name: House Stark
description: Seat of ancient power, where the direwolf's howl carries across a thousand years of ice and blood. House Stark has ruled the North since the Age of Heroes, their roots entwined with the very permafrost of their domain. Stoic, honorable, and fiercely loyal, the Starks are the conscience of Westeros — a conscience the realm cannot afford to lose. They bind their bannermen not through fear but through the patient accumulation of justice delivered consistently across generations.
wordsExplanation: Most houses boast of strength or glory; the Starks remind themselves of mortality. 'Winter Is Coming' is not a threat but a philosophy — a perpetual readiness, a refusal to be lulled by summer's comfort. It is why the North survives when softer kingdoms fail.
arc: From Lord Eddard's execution that shattered the realm's illusions of honorable governance, through the Red Wedding's devastation of the Stark line, to the triumphant survival of every surviving Stark child — Sansa as Queen in the North, Arya sailing west, Bran ruling the Six Kingdoms, Jon exiled and finally free. The wolf endured. The North remembered.
history: Founded by Bran the Builder, who raised both Winterfell and the Wall itself, House Stark has endured ice age and summer drought alike. For eight thousand years they held dominion over the North, bending knee only once — to Aegon the Conqueror. The War of the Five Kings nearly extinguished their ancient flame, when Lord Eddard Stark's honor led him to the executioner's block and Robb Stark's justice led him to the Red Wedding. Yet the Stark lineage proved impossible to extinguish. Through Sansa, the political inheritor; Jon, the secret Targaryen blood; and Arya, death's own instrument — the wolf endures.

name: House Lannister
description: The richest house in all the Seven Kingdoms, their gold mines beneath Casterly Rock once seemed inexhaustible as their ambition. A Lannister always pays his debts — the most famous unofficial words in Westeros, spoken by men who understand that power is nothing without the will to use it mercilessly. They project strength even in weakness, and the facade has served them almost as well as the gold itself. Their lion sigil declares what they believe themselves to be: apex predators in a realm of prey.
wordsExplanation: 'Hear Me Roar' speaks to their self-image — they demand to be noticed, feared, and obeyed. Yet the Lannisters are defined more by their unofficial words, 'A Lannister Always Pays His Debts,' which acknowledges that their power rests on reputation for consequence, not just wealth. The lion roars but the ledger is what kingdoms fear.
arc: Tywin Lannister raised his house to its zenith through decades of ruthless statecraft, only for his three children to unravel it through sin, grief, and wine. Cersei's wildfire ambition consumed Tommen and the dynasty. Jaime died with the woman he could never leave. Only Tyrion survived — Hand to a king no one expected, writing history with the very hands his father wished had never existed.
history: House Lannister traces its lineage to Lann the Clever, the legendary trickster of the Age of Heroes who swindled Casterly Rock from its previous owners through cunning alone. Their golden lions have cast long shadows across Westeros: Tywin Lannister's sack of King's Landing ended the Mad King's reign, and his political machinations shaped the realm for decades. The twin sins of Cersei and Jaime's union secretly placed bastard blood upon the Iron Throne. The Lannister golden age crested under Tywin and collapsed spectacularly under his children — pride being the ancient enemy of every lion.

name: House Targaryen
description: They came from Old Valyria with fire and dragons, and for nearly three centuries they sat upon the Iron Throne they forged from the swords of their enemies. The blood of old Valyria runs through their veins — platinum hair, violet eyes, and a peculiar affinity for fire that borders on madness. They do not burn. They are the dragon. Every Targaryen king walked the razor's edge between greatness and catastrophe, and the history of the realm is largely the record of which side of that edge they fell on.
wordsExplanation: 'Fire and Blood' is not an aspiration but a historical record — both how the Targaryens took the realm and what they left behind when they held it badly. It acknowledges that their power is absolute and absolutely dangerous. The words speak with the confidence of a people who believe themselves to be beyond consequence.
arc: From Aegon the Conqueror's unification of the realm under dragonfire to the Doom of House Targaryen in Robert's Rebellion, and then the remarkable second act of Daenerys Targaryen's decades-long campaign to reclaim the throne — only to destroy herself in the moment of victory by giving in to the madness her bloodline carries. The last dragon flew east with her body. The dynasty ended.
history: Aegon the Conqueror unified six of the Seven Kingdoms through dragonfire and diplomacy, forging the Iron Throne from the swords of his defeated enemies. For nearly three hundred years, Targaryens ruled Westeros — their reign marked by brilliant statecraft and catastrophic madness in equal measure. The Dance of the Dragons consumed their greatest weapons; the Mad King Aerys II squandered their legacy until Robert's Rebellion ended Targaryen rule in a welter of blood. Daenerys Targaryen crossed the Narrow Sea with fire and fury to reclaim what was taken, only to lose herself to the very madness that felled her father.

name: House Baratheon
description: Forged in storm and fury, House Baratheon rose from the bastard line of House Targaryen. They are warriors made flesh — broad-shouldered, black-haired, bellowing men who govern with iron fists and iron will. Robert Baratheon's war hammer ended the Targaryen dynasty and placed the stag upon the throne, yet his own house could not survive his death. The fury that won them everything proved incapable of the patience required to hold it.
wordsExplanation: 'Ours Is the Fury' captures the Baratheon essence: unrestrained, instinctive, and entirely confident in its own righteousness. The fury is their inheritance from the Targaryen blood they share, transformed into something blunter and more honest. Where Targaryens wielded fire with purpose, Baratheons bludgeon with rage.
arc: Robert Baratheon won the realm with a war hammer and spent seventeen years drinking it away. His death set three brothers against each other: Joffrey (not his son), Stannis (righteous and doomed), and Renly (charming and equally doomed). All perished. The stag house passed into history with nothing to show for their fury but the broken wheel that a Targaryen girl would claim she could fix.
history: House Baratheon was founded by Orys Baratheon, Aegon the Conqueror's rumored bastard half-brother, who received the Stormlands as his reward for conquest. For generations they ruled their storm-wracked keep with distinction. Robert Baratheon's rebellion against the Mad King united the realm's great lords in common cause, and for seventeen years Robert held the Seven Kingdoms together through force of personality alone. His death split his brothers: the dutiful Stannis, who had the best claim, and the charming Renly, who had the best army. Both perished, and with them the true Baratheon line.

name: House Tyrell
description: From the most fertile lands in Westeros, the Tyrells cultivated not only crops but influence. Highgarden is the garden of the realm — all beauty, abundance, and dangerous thorns beneath the roses. The Tyrells understood that the power to feed a kingdom is the power to rule it. Their political marriages, their beautiful children, and their ruthless dowager matriarch made them the most reliably successful political house of the modern era — until wildfire rendered all their cultivation to ash in a single emerald moment.
wordsExplanation: 'Growing Strong' is the most deceptively humble of house words — it speaks not of current greatness but of incremental accumulation. The Tyrells never claimed to be the strongest, only to be always becoming stronger. It is the philosophy of the patient climber, and for generations it served them better than any boast.
arc: From ambitious newcomers seeking greater relevance through marriage to the most powerful non-ruling house in Westeros — and then annihilated in seconds. Cersei's wildfire under the Great Sept killed Margaery, Loras, and Mace Tyrell simultaneously. Lady Olenna — the Queen of Thorns — died alone in her seat with the satisfaction of confessing to Joffrey's murder with a smile.
history: The Tyrells rose as stewards to House Gardener, the ancient Kings of the Reach, and inherited their seat through administrative competence rather than conquest. Lady Olenna Tyrell — the Queen of Thorns — was their true sovereign power for decades, orchestrating alliances, marriages, and when necessary, quiet murders to advance the family's position. Margaery Tyrell married three kings in succession, her beauty and political instincts making her the most valuable piece on the chessboard. The Great Sept's wildfire ended the Tyrell line in a moment of emerald flame.

name: House Martell
description: Dorne alone refused to kneel to dragonfire. Alone among the great houses, the Martells preserved their independence through guerrilla warfare and the simple lesson that a dragon cannot hold what it has burned. Their words are not mere boast — they are historical record written in Targaryen blood. They practice equal inheritance regardless of gender, permit bastard children their dignity, and produce a people whose capacity for a long, patient grudge is legendary even by Westerosi standards.
wordsExplanation: 'Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken' is simultaneously a historical fact and a perpetual vow. The Martells never bowed to Aegon's dragons, never bent to Targaryen demands for submission, and emerged from every war unbroken. It is also the credo that drove Oberyn Martell into a fight he nearly won — the refusal to let injustice go unanswered, no matter the personal cost.
arc: From their unique historical stance as the only kingdom to join Westeros by choice rather than conquest, to the tragedy of Princess Elia's murder poisoning Dornish politics for a generation, to Oberyn Martell's spectacular near-victory and defeat in King's Landing. Dorne's vengeance was ultimately completed by Ellaria Sand's poison — a weapon worthy of a house that values patience over spectacle.
history: House Martell is unique among the great houses for having never been conquered by Aegon the Conqueror — their resistance led by Princess Meria and later Deria Martell, who delivered such a devastating psychological blow to Aegon that he abandoned the conquest of Dorne entirely. They joined the Seven Kingdoms through marriage, not submission, retaining their prince's title rather than accepting a lord's. The murder of Princess Elia Martell during the Sack of King's Landing left a wound that never healed — Oberyn Martell's poisoned spear and Ellaria Sand's patient revenge both flow from that single act of barbarity.

name: House Tully
description: At the confluence of rivers sits Riverrun, its red walls rising from the waters like a salmon fighting upstream. The Tullys are lords of the crossroads — geographically, politically, and morally. Their words are a hierarchy of obligations that has guided and occasionally trapped them for generations. Family before duty, duty before honor — each a level that must be satisfied before the next can be reached, making them simultaneously the most loyal and most predictable of the great houses.
wordsExplanation: 'Family, Duty, Honor' establishes a moral hierarchy that defined Catelyn Stark's every decision and eventually Edmure Tully's final surrender. Family comes first — a declaration that the Tullys will sacrifice abstract principles for concrete people. This made them compassionate rulers and occasionally disastrous strategists.
arc: From the center of the War of the Five Kings — the Riverlands being the most fought-over territory in Westeros — to Catelyn's death at the Red Wedding, to Edmure's long imprisonment by the Lannisters. House Tully survived but diminished, the salmon's upstream battle ending in a prisoner's cell rather than glory. Edmure was eventually freed and House Tully endured, bruised and depleted.
history: House Tully rose to prominence as Lords Paramount of the Trident after supporting Aegon the Conqueror's campaign. Hoster Tully's political marriages connected the great houses of the realm in a web that proved both his family's greatest asset and most dangerous liability: his daughter Catelyn's marriage to Eddard Stark drew the North into the War of the Five Kings, while his daughter Lysa's political maneuvering fed the very chaos that consumed the realm. Riverrun itself — the moated fortress where three rivers meet — has changed hands more times in its history than any other great castle in Westeros.

name: House Arryn
description: No castle in all of Westeros sits closer to the gods than the Eyrie, perched impossibly upon the peaks of the Giant's Lance. The Arryns are as cold and pure as mountain air — ancient, proud, and utterly convinced of their own righteousness. Their judgment, like their keep, admits no easy approach. The Moon Door beneath the throne room — a hole in the floor through which the unwanted are ejected into the mountain air — speaks to both the Arryn sense of justice and their very literal perspective on consequences.
wordsExplanation: 'As High as Honor' captures the Arryn self-image: they aspire to moral elevation matching their geographical one. The Eyrie sits literally above all rivals, and the Arryns believe their ethics to be equally elevated. Whether this conviction has been consistently justified by their actions is a question the moon door does not pause to consider.
arc: Jon Arryn's murder at Lysa's poisoned hand — orchestrated by Littlefinger — set the entire series of wars in motion. The Vale stayed neutral through most of the War of the Five Kings, its knight-armies preserved while others spent theirs. It was the Vale's cavalry that saved Jon Snow at the Battle of the Bastards. Robin Arryn ultimately survived and grew into his seat, the most underestimated survivor of the entire game.
history: Among the oldest noble houses in Westeros, the Arryns claim descent from the First Men who survived the Long Night. As the principal house of the Vale, they maintained the Mountain Clans below and the clouds above with equal authority. Jon Arryn served as Hand of the King to Robert Baratheon, his discovery of Joffrey's parentage setting the entire series of wars in motion before his murder — by his own wife's hand, administered through poison purchased by Littlefinger. The Vale's strategic isolation allowed it to stay largely neutral in the great wars, its power preserved when others were spent.

name: House Greyjoy
description: From the storm-lashed Iron Islands, the Greyjoys reign over a people who believe in taking what others have built. Salt and iron, reaving and raiding — this is the Old Way, the Drowned God's way. They do not sow because they believe themselves above the labor of growth. All things come to those willing to reach out and take them. The Iron Islands breed men who mistake cruelty for strength and confuse the absence of peace with the presence of purpose.
wordsExplanation: 'We Do Not Sow' is the most brutally honest of house words — a frank acknowledgment that ironborn culture is parasitic. They take what others grow, build, and protect. It is simultaneously a boast and a confession, spoken by a people who have weaponized their own poverty into an identity.
arc: Theon Greyjoy's journey from ward to betrayer to broken man to redeemed hero forms the most complete character arc in the series. Yara Greyjoy's steady leadership. Euron Greyjoy's nihilistic ascent to maximum destruction. The iron islands remained standing after everything, but their greatest son died alone charging the Night King at Winterfell — the only death that gave him back his name.
history: The Iron Islands have a history older than the Seven Kingdoms, rooted in the culture of ironborn reavers who once raided as far as Oldtown. House Greyjoy rose atop this tradition to rule the islands. Balon Greyjoy's rebellion against Robert Baratheon was crushed decisively, and his sons Rodrik and Maron died in the assault on Seagard, leaving only Theon as ward-hostage. Balon's ill-timed second rebellion during the War of the Five Kings began well but ended in Theon's capture, psychological destruction, and ultimate redemption. Euron Greyjoy's return shifted everything — a captain without conscience, wielding a horn that binds dragons.

name: House Bolton
description: The ancient enemies of House Stark, the Boltons once flayed their enemies and wore their skins as cloaks. That practice was supposedly outlawed centuries ago. The flayed man on their banner suggests old habits die slowly. Their seat — the Dreadfort — is a name that has frightened northern children to sleep for a thousand years. The house represents the darkness that honor was invented to hold at bay — and what happens when that darkness is given a castle, a fleet, and letters of nobility.
wordsExplanation: 'Our Blades Are Sharp' is the most uncomfortably literal of house words — a direct reference to the flaying knives their ancestors wielded as instruments of governance. It is a threat worn openly, which in its own terrible way is more honest than houses who cloak their violence in prettier language.
arc: Roose Bolton's cold, calculating betrayal at the Red Wedding delivered him everything he wanted. Ramsay Bolton exceeded even his father's cruelty, systematically destroying Theon Greyjoy and brutalizing Sansa Stark. Their house ended appropriately: Ramsay died in his own kennels, consumed by his own hounds in the presence of the woman he had broken and failed to break. Justice, North-style.
history: House Bolton's history is one of opportunistic brutality. For millennia they fought the Starks for dominance of the North, and for millennia they lost. Roose Bolton's calculated betrayal at the Red Wedding, where he personally drove a blade through Robb Stark's heart, delivered him Wardenship of the North. His bastard son Ramsay proved even more monstrous — a man who hunted people for sport and took pleasure in psychological destruction as much as physical. Their house ended when Ramsay died in the kennels, consumed by the very hounds he had starved.

name: House Frey
description: Walder Frey built his house's power on the one asset geography gave him — a bridge. The Crossing of the Green Fork gave the Freys leverage over every army marching north or south. A toll collector's descendants became lords, then kingmakers, then betrayers whose name became synonymous with dishonor throughout all of Westeros. The violation of guest right at the Red Wedding was not just a crime against the Starks — it was an offense against the gods themselves, and the gods have long memories.
wordsExplanation: 'We Stand Together' is the most ironic of house words given their history of betrayal. The Freys stood together at the Red Wedding — all of them complicit, all of them murderers. The words speak to family solidarity but the actions speak to a people who have redefined solidarity as collective villainy.
arc: The Red Wedding secured the Freys everything they wanted — power, prestige, marriage into noble lines — and within two seasons cost them everything. Arya Stark's systematic culling of the Frey line, climaxing in the poisoning of every Frey lord at a feast, was one of the most complete acts of vengeance in the series. The North remembered. So did the gods.
history: House Frey achieved prominence through control of the Twins, the only crossing of the Green Fork for miles in either direction. For generations they used this geographical advantage to extract concessions and marriages from houses who needed to pass. Walder Frey's perceived slight — that Robb Stark reneged on his promise to marry a Frey daughter — became the justification for the Red Wedding, an act that violated the sacred laws of guest right. The surviving Freys were systematically poisoned by Arya Stark wearing the face of Walder himself, leaving no Frey lord alive to carry the legacy forward.

name: House Mormont
description: From the cold, rocky shores of Bear Island — where even the trees grow at a grudging angle against the wind — House Mormont produces men and women who have never needed anyone to confirm their worth. Smaller than a dozen other northern houses, they carry more moral authority than any. The women of Bear Island learned to fight alongside the men generations ago, when ironborn raiders came in the night and there were only women and children left to meet them. That tradition produced Lyanna Mormont, who shamed lords thirty times her age into action with a ten-year-old's contempt.
wordsExplanation: 'Here We Stand' is the declaration of a house that will not retreat, will not compromise, and will not be moved. Bear Island has no strategic value that would justify the ferocity with which the Mormonts have always defended it. They stand because standing is simply what they do. The words are three syllables of pure northern stubbornness.
arc: Jeor Mormont served as Lord Commander of the Night's Watch and died beyond the Wall in a mutiny at Craster's Keep. Ser Jorah Mormont was exiled for selling men into slavery, spent years searching for redemption through service to Daenerys, and died defending Bran Stark at Winterfell. Young Lyanna Mormont shamed the North's lords into action and died in the jaws of a wight giant, driving a dragonglass blade into its eye as she fell. House Mormont fought in every critical battle and died in almost all of them.
history: House Mormont has sworn fealty to House Stark for as long as either house has existed. Bear Island, a remote and frequently raided outpost in the far northwest of the North, produced a military culture by necessity. The women of Bear Island received combat training equal to men — a tradition born of ironborn raids when the men were away fishing. Jeor Mormont resigned his lordship to take the black, passing the seat to his disgraced son Jorah. When Jorah was exiled, Maege Mormont and then her daughter Lyanna held Bear Island with quiet ferocity.

name: House Reed
description: The crannogmen of the Neck are the most mysterious people in all of Westeros — small, green-eyed, and deeply in tune with the wetlands they call home. House Reed rules from Greywater Watch, a castle that moves with the currents of the swamp and has never been found by any enemy. Lord Howland Reed is perhaps the most important man alive — the sole surviving witness to what happened at the Tower of Joy, and the keeper of the most consequential secret in the realm. He attended the first Westerosi tournament as a youth and was the first person to show young Eddard Stark what honor actually costs.
wordsExplanation: 'Hearth and Harvest and Hall' speaks to a simpler, older value system — the three pillars of sustainable civilization as the crannogmen understand it. Not glory, not conquest, not honor in the abstract — but warmth, food, and shelter. The crannogmen have survived by being exactly as unglamorous and indestructible as their words suggest.
arc: Howland Reed fought beside Eddard Stark at the Tower of Joy and has kept the secret of Jon Snow's parentage for nearly twenty years. His children Jojen and Meera guided Bran Stark north of the Wall to reach the Three-Eyed Raven. Jojen died in that service. Meera brought Bran home alive. House Reed paid its debts to House Stark in full and more.
history: The crannogmen predate the Andal invasion and the unification of Westeros, maintaining ancient customs and a connection to the Children of the Forest that most of the realm long abandoned. Howland Reed became one of Eddard Stark's most trusted companions, fighting alongside him in Robert's Rebellion and at the Tower of Joy. His knowledge of what transpired in that tower — the truth of Jon Snow's birth — made him the most dangerous man in the realm, a danger he exercised with absolute silence for decades.

name: House Karstark
description: A cadet branch of House Stark, claiming descent from Karlon Stark who was granted his own seat thousands of years ago. The Karstarks are northmen in the truest sense — harder than stone, slower to anger than a glacier, and considerably more dangerous when their anger finally comes. They raised their banners for Robb Stark and marched south in the first flush of the War of the Five Kings. Robb Stark's execution of Lord Rickard Karstark for murdering Lannister prisoners split their house in half and contributed decisively to the King in the North's eventual defeat.
wordsExplanation: 'The Sun of Winter' captures the paradox of northern existence — the way a single moment of light and warmth means everything to those who live most of their lives in cold and darkness. The sun of winter is brief, precious, and blinding precisely because it is so rare. The Karstarks are that light: fierce, loyal, and briefly magnificent before the dark closes in.
arc: Rickard Karstark's grief-maddened murder of Lannister boy hostages and Robb Stark's honorable but catastrophic decision to execute him for it cost the Northern cause half its forces. Most Karstark men subsequently joined Ramsay Bolton. Alys Karstark's political marriage to Sigorn of the Wildlings secured new alliances and preserved the house's independence into the next era.
history: House Karstark descends from Karlon Stark, a son of House Stark who was given lands in the east of the North for his service. For millennia they have been among the most reliable Stark bannermen. Rickard Karstark raised 2,000 men for Robb Stark and marched them south. When his sons died in battle — Torrhen killed in single combat, Eddard captured and executed — grief unmade him. He murdered two Lannister squire-prisoners in revenge. Robb executed him. The consequences rippled outward for seasons.

name: House Umber
description: The northernmost of the great northern houses, the Umbers hold the Last Hearth at the very edge of the settled world — a day's ride from the Wall, with nothing between them and the land beyond but cold and old superstition. They are the Night's Watch's nearest neighbors among the nobility, which has given them a healthy respect for what lies beyond the Wall and an unhealthy comfort with its proximity. The Greatjon Umber was perhaps the most physically impressive lord in the North — a man who called Robb Stark a boy to his face, had two fingers bitten off by Grey Wind, and then laughed and named Robb his king.
wordsExplanation: 'Strength in Service' declares that the Umbers understand power differently from houses who seek to accumulate it — they believe strength is best expressed in service to something greater than themselves. This philosophy made the Greatjon Umber one of Robb Stark's most committed bannermen, and the betrayal of young Ned Umber who handed Rickon Stark to Ramsay Bolton all the more devastating.
arc: The Greatjon Umber was captured at the Red Wedding and died in captivity. Young Ned Umber's decision to hand Rickon Stark to Ramsay Bolton — whether from fear, pragmatism, or true betrayal — hastened Rickon's death. Ned Umber himself was killed by the Night King at the Last Hearth and raised as a wight, the first sign that the dead had crossed the Wall. House Umber ended as it began: at the very edge of the world, facing what comes from the dark.
history: The Umbers have held the Last Hearth since time immemorial — the seat closest to the Wall of any great house. Their lords have traditionally been massive men who match the harshness of their lands. The Greatjon Umber — Lord Jon Umber — challenged Robb Stark's authority at the war council before Robb's wolves bit off his fingers, after which the Greatjon laughed and declared Robb the best man there. He was captured at the Red Wedding. His heir Smalljon died there. Young Ned Umber surrendered the house's last Stark ward to Ramsay Bolton, sealing his own fate.

name: House Clegane
description: Not truly a great house — more a very recent family elevation, born three generations ago when a kennelmaster named Clegane saved Lord Tywin Lannister's father from a lion at the cost of three fingers and an eye. The Cleganes were given a keep and a knighthood for that service. Two generations produced the greatest and most brutal knight in Westeros (Gregor, the Mountain), and the most reluctant and compelling moral rehabilitation in the series (Sandor, the Hound). The keep is small. The legacy is enormous.
wordsExplanation: House Clegane has no official words — they are too new and too minor a house for the formal traditions. They were raised by a single act of loyal service, and both brothers defined their lives in response to that origin: Gregor by embodying everything a knight should be feared as, Sandor by refusing to pretend the institution meant anything.
arc: Gregor Clegane's career is a catalogue of atrocity — rapist, murderer, terror. He was poisoned by Oberyn Martell, revived as something that was no longer alive by Qyburn, and finally destroyed in the Red Keep by his own brother. Sandor Clegane traveled the longest moral road of any character — from the Hound to a man who could sit with a septon and consider what he had done. His Cleganebowl death was both inevitable and chosen.
history: House Clegane was elevated three generations past when the Clegane kennelmaster saved Lord Tywin's father from a rogue lion during a hunt. He was granted knighthood, a keep, and lands. The first generation of Clegane knights served dutifully. The second produced Gregor — who was given his first command and celebrated with a massacre — and Sandor, whom Gregor burned as a child for playing with one of his toys. The house died with both brothers.

name: House Tarth
description: The Sapphire Isle — so called for the clear blue waters that surround it — is a gentle land of waterfalls and fishing villages that has somehow produced the greatest knight of her generation. Brienne of Tarth is House Tarth's greatest achievement and its greatest embarrassment to those who could not see past her gender, a woman who could have chosen comfort and chose instead to be worthy of the knights in the stories she loved. Lord Selwyn Tarth, her father, was always quietly proud. He gave her the best masters-at-arms he could find and asked no questions about why.
wordsExplanation: 'Our Honor, Our Sword' collapses the traditional knightly values into a single equation: honor and combat are inseparable. You cannot have one without the other — an honorable knight who will not fight is useless; a fighter without honor is a criminal. Brienne Tarth embodies these words more completely than any hereditary warrior in her generation.
arc: House Tarth produced Brienne, who pledged herself to causes rather than lords and was knighted by Jaime Lannister in the hour before the Battle of Winterfell. She fulfilled every pledge she ever made — to Renly's memory, to Catelyn Stark, to Sansa and Arya, to the living against the dead. She loved Jaime Lannister and could not save him from himself. She wrote his story in the White Book with a knight's honesty.
history: House Tarth has served House Baratheon of Storm's End for generations, their island off the coast of the Stormlands providing both fish and levied soldiers to the lords of the region. Selwyn Tarth raised Brienne as his heir in the absence of other children, providing her combat training despite the scandal it created. Brienne's career made the Tarth name known across the realm — both for her skill and for her unlikely knighthood at Jaime Lannister's hands.
